hints: Focus on the carbonate ion alone and think what oxide ion and neutral gas it can split into while keeping atoms and charge balanced.
walkthrough:
Picture what decomposition means**
Think of the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion breaking into two pieces. One piece stays in the solid as the oxide ion, $\text{O}^{2-}$, and the other escapes as a gas, carbon dioxide, $\text{CO}_2$. No metal ion is involved here because you are writing the ionic change only.

Check atoms and charge**
Count through: one C and three O on each side, and $2-$ charge on each side. So $\text{CO}_3^{2-} \rightarrow \text{O}^{2-} + \text{CO}_2$ is already balanced for both mass and charge.

hints: Recall whether $\text{MgCO}_3$ decomposes more easily on heating than $\text{BaCO}_3$ to decide if stability increases or decreases down Group 2.
Compare the size of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and think how ionic radius changes with increasing atomic number down the group.
Link the charge density of the $2+$ cation to its ability to distort the electron cloud of the large $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion.
walkthrough:
State the observed trend clearly**
Picture heating $\text{MgCO}_3$ and $\text{BaCO}_3$. Magnesium carbonate decomposes very easily while barium carbonate needs much stronger heating. So stability increases going down Group 2 as atomic number increases.

Track the size of the cation**
All Group 2 ions carry the same $2+$ charge, but the ion gets larger down the group because extra electron shells are added. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is small and compact, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is much larger. Larger radius means the same charge is spread over a bigger volume, so charge density falls.

See how a small cation weakens the carbonate**
Imagine a tiny, highly charging $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ pulling hard on the electrons of a neighbouring $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion. It distorts or polarises the carbonate, weakening a C-O bond and helping it break into $\text{O}^{2-}$ and $\text{CO}_2$. That is why decomposition is easy.

Explain why larger cations are more stable**
A large cation such as $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ has low polarising power. It distorts the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion much less, the C-O bonds stay stronger, and much more thermal energy is needed to force decomposition. Hence thermal stability increases down the group.

Final answer: Thermal stability increases down Group 2 with increasing atomic number.
Down the group cationic radius increases / ion size increases.
Larger cation has lower charge density so causes less polarisation / distortion of the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion, so more heat is needed to decompose it.

hints: Look up the ionic radii of the $2+$ ions in the Data Booklet and compare $\text{Pb}^{2+}$, $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ by size.
Apply the same polarisation idea as for Group 2: the smallest $2+$ ion will distort $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ most and give the least stable carbonate.
walkthrough:
Pull out the key data**
Stability here is still controlled by cation size. From the Data Booklet: $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ is 0.120 nm, $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is 0.099 nm, $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ is 0.075 nm. All are $2+$ ions, so size alone decides polarising power.

Rank polarising power**
$\text{Zn}^{2+}$ is the smallest, so it has the highest charge density and polarises $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ most strongly. $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ is the largest, so it polarises least. $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ sits in the middle.

Predict the stability order**
Least distortion means most stable. So the largest cation gives the most stable carbonate: (most stable) $\text{PbCO}_3$ > $\text{CaCO}_3$ > $\text{ZnCO}_3$ (least stable).

Final answer: data: ($\text{Pb}^{2+}$) 0.120 nm; ($\text{Ca}^{2+}$) 0.099 nm; ($\text{Zn}^{2+}$) 0.075 nm
(most stable) $\text{PbCO}_3$ > $\text{CaCO}_3$ > $\text{ZnCO}_3$ (least stable)

hints: Convert the volume of $\text{CO}_2$ to moles using the room conditions molar volume, $24000 \text{ cm}^3 \text{ mol}^{-1}$, and remember to keep volume in $\text{cm}^3$.
Write the reaction of $\text{CaMg(CO}_3)_2$ with $\text{HCl}$ and use the 1:2 ratio of carbonate to $\text{CO}_2$ to find moles of double carbonate.
Multiply moles of $\text{CaMg(CO}_3)_2$ by its $M_r$ of about 184.4 to get mass present, then express this as a percentage of the 0.642 g sample.
walkthrough:
Convert gas volume to moles**
Only the carbonate produces $\text{CO}_2$, impurities do nothing. Under room conditions one mole of gas occupies $24000 \text{ cm}^3$:
$$n(\text{CO}_2) = \frac{V}{24000} = \frac{125.0}{24000} = 5.21 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

Use stoichiometry to find moles of dolomite**
The double carbonate contains two carbonate groups:
$$\text{CaMg(CO}_3)_2 + 4\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + \text{MgCl}_2 + 2\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
So 1 mol of $\text{CaMg(CO}_3)_2$ gives 2 mol of $\text{CO}_2$:
$$n(\text{CaMg(CO}_3)_2) = \frac{5.21 \times 10^{-3}}{2} = 2.60 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

Convert to mass and percentage**
$M_r$ of $\text{CaMg(CO}_3)_2 = 40.1 + 24.3 + 2 \times (12.0 + 3 \times 16.0) = 184.4$:
$$m = n \times M_r = 2.60 \times 10^{-3} \times 184.4 = 0.480 \text{ g}$$
$$\% = \frac{0.480}{0.642} \times 100 = 74.8\%$$

Final answer: amount of $\text{CO}_2 = 125 / 24000 = 5.21 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$
$\text{CaMg(CO}_3)_2 : \text{CO}_2 = 1:2$, amount of carbonate $= 5.21 \times 10^{-3} / 2 = 2.60 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$
mass $= 184.4 \times 2.60 \times 10^{-3} = 0.480 \text{ g}$
% $= 100 \times 0.480 / 0.642 = 74.8$ %
